blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Repetition counting requires identifying and enumerating action cycles over time. While state-of-the-art video language models describe actions fluently, they fail to reliably count how many times an action repeats. To investigate this limitation, we introduce RepProbe, a benchmark of 42K real and synthetic video clips containing exactly k in [1, 20] complete repetitions, with controls for clip position, temporal coverage, and duration. These controls allow us to study the counting failure directly and locate where in the model it arises. Counting accuracy collapses at high counts across the video language models we evaluate, and controlled experiments show this collapse is not explained by frame sampling alone. We compare model outputs with linear probes trained on the final-layer representations used to generate those outputs. We find a consistent representation-to-output dissociation: substantial count information remains linearly decodable even when models fail to report the correct count. Further analysis shows this failure arises primarily at the output stage, where answers concentrate on a small set of preferred numbers rather than the available count information. The dissociation holds on both real and synthetic videos and is not explained by clip duration, position, or scene content. These results indicate that models encode repetition structure but do not reliably report it in their outputs. Project page: https://arenaa.github.io/RepProbe-webpage/

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Counting how many times an action repeats is a basic temporal skill. It
requires identifying discrete action instances, recognizing the cycles of a
periodic action, and accumulating these repetitions as they unfold over time.
Unlike static counting, these repetitions are distributed across a sequence,
so no single moment contains the answer. Human cognition treats this capacity
as distinct: the number of sequential events is represented separately from
other temporal properties such as duration ( White, 1963 ) , and
parietal populations encode how many times an action is repeated
independently of the action’s identity ( Sawamura et al., 2020 ) . Counting
therefore differs from recognizing an action. Recognition, even when it
requires temporal information, is a categorical judgment about presence or
identity; counting tracks each occurrence and accumulates them into an exact
quantity. This makes repetition counting a precise test of whether a model
tracks temporal structure, and it is also required in practice, for instance
in exercise and rehabilitation monitoring, where approximate counts are of
limited use ( Dwibedi et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) .

blocks.en:
Video Language Models (VLMs) handle this task poorly. They describe repetitive
actions fluently yet misreport how many times the actions occur, and their
error grows with the number of repetitions ( Yao et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . The
difficulty does not lie in the task itself: specialist counters trained for
this purpose remain accurate at high counts, whereas general-purpose video
language models, despite their scale and broad video training, degrade as
repetitions accumulate. Existing evaluations of counting and related temporal
skills ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Cores et al., 2024 ; Patraucean et al., 2023 ) ,
however, measure only the final answer, and they do not separate repetition
count from factors that vary with it, such as clip duration, temporal
coverage, and source video. An incorrect answer does not imply that the
underlying information is absent: probing studies show that models can encode
information they do not express ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Burns et al., 2022 ; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023 ) . The
source of the failure therefore remains open: do these models fail to
represent the count, or represent it but fail to report it? The answer
matters, because a failure of representation and a failure of readout call
for different remedies.

blocks.en:
To address this question, we introduce RepProbe , a diagnostic
benchmark in which every clip contains an exact, known number of complete
repetitions. In RepCount ( Hu et al., 2022 ) , each video carries a single
count entangled with its duration and source. RepProbe-Real instead cuts clips
with exactly k k repetitions from each RepCount source video, controlling clip
position and source-level splits while auditing duration and temporal
coverage. RepProbe-Synthetic is a controlled set, balanced across counts, in
which only a single attribute changes periodically. We evaluate seven open
video language models and two specialist counters on RepProbe. To test whether
the count is absent from the model or present but not reported, we then
compare two readouts of the count from the same final-layer state of the
strongest generalists: the model’s generated answer, and a linear probe on the
representation consumed by the language head. Finally, we test whether the
decodable count reflects the repetitions themselves, using duration and
clip-position controls on real video and controlled synthetic stimuli.

Our results show that the count is represented within the
model but not faithfully reported. Generalist
video language models count reasonably well at low counts but collapse at high
counts, where a specialist counter remains accurate, and this collapse is not
explained by frame sampling. Yet the count remains linearly decodable from the
final-layer state that the language head reads, even when the model’s answer
is wrong. This dissociation also holds on synthetic stimuli, and it is not explained by duration or clip position. The generated answers instead concentrate on a small set
of preferred numbers, largely independent of the true count. These findings
indicate that the high-count failure of video language models arises in the
readout of the representation rather than in the representation itself. Our
analysis complements prior work showing that probes can recover temporal
information from vision-side features ( Li et al., 2025 ) : we localize the
gap to the final representation consumed by the language head, and show that
it widens as the count grows.

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Repetitive action counting has been studied as a dedicated video understanding
problem. Early approaches estimate repetition periods from temporal
self-similarity (RepNet; Dwibedi et al. 2020 ), while later methods
address unknown and varying cycle lengths through context-aware,
scale-insensitive estimation ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) . Datasets progressed
from Countix ( Dwibedi et al., 2020 ) and UCFRep ( Zhang et al., 2020 ) to RepCount, which introduces variable-length videos
and fine-grained cycle annotations, together with density-map supervision for
repetition-period estimation ( Hu et al., 2022 ) . Recent specialist
counters include Every Shot Counts (ESCounts), which uses exemplar-based
visual correspondence across repetitions ( Sinha et al., 2024 ) , PAMS, a
self-supervised method based on period-adaptive multi-scale consistency ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and multimodal methods that combine appearance and pose
to model repetitive motion under background variation ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . These methods are trained for counting and optimize
counting accuracy. Together, they establish repetition counting as a
well-defined video understanding target with a measurable ground-truth
quantity, making it a controlled setting for testing whether general-purpose
video language models encode the information needed for counting.

blocks.en:
Counting remains challenging for vision-language models even on static images ( Acharya et al., 2018 ; Paiss et al., 2023 ) , and
recent perception benchmarks continue to identify failures on basic visual
counting and spatial tasks ( Rahmanzadehgervi et al., 2024 ; Fu et al., 2024 ) .
In video, counting becomes temporal, since events must be accumulated across
frames. Video benchmarks such as MVBench include temporal action-understanding
tasks ( Li et al., 2024b ) , while CountLLM ( Yao et al., 2025 ) and the
exercise-counting benchmark PushupBench ( Li et al., 2026 ) report
substantial difficulties for general-purpose video language models on repetition
counting. More broadly, benchmarks evaluate fine-grained temporal ( Li et al., 2024b ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , long-form ( Wu et al., 2024 ) , and visual-temporal reasoning ( Shangguan et al., 2025 ) , but existing evaluations can still admit
solutions based on a few frames or without preserving temporal order.
RepProbe makes repetition count the controlled temporal variable and audits
alternative cues such as temporal position, sampling, duration, and source.
Whereas these benchmarks primarily measure failure at the output, RepProbe
localizes it by testing whether count information is absent from the
representation or present but not surfaced by the model’s native output.

blocks.en:
Linear probing provides a standard way to measure whether task-relevant
information is recoverable from frozen representations ( Alain and Bengio, 2016 ; Belinkov, 2022 ) , and has shown that LLMs
linearly encode structured quantities such as space, time, truth, and numeric
value ( Gurnee and Tegmark, 2024 ; Marks and Tegmark, 2023 ; Heinzerling and Inui, 2024 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . Prior work has also shown that probes can recover
information that is not reliably expressed in model outputs ( Burns et al., 2022 ; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023 ; Orgad et al., 2025 ) , with related
work finding similar gaps in vision-language models ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) . Interpretability studies of video LLMs further examine
where visual and temporal information is integrated across layers ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Shi et al., 2025 ) . However, decodability does not
imply that the model uses the information ( Ravichander et al., 2021 ; Elazar et al., 2021 ) . We therefore do not treat
probe accuracy as evidence of capability: the probe tests whether count
information is decodable from a representation, which we compare directly
with the information surfaced by the model’s native language head. This
distinction is particularly relevant to recent work showing that temporal
information can be decoded from video representations even when Video LLMs
perform poorly on corresponding temporal reasoning tasks ( Li et al., 2025 ) . Whereas that work probes an earlier vision-side
representation, we examine the final-layer vector directly consumed by the
language head.

blocks.en: 3 The RepProbe Benchmark
blocks.zh: 3 备用基准

blocks.en:
Existing repetition-counting benchmarks such as RepCount ( Hu et al., 2022 ) were designed to train and evaluate specialist counters, and they are not
suited to diagnosing why a model miscounts. Each RepCount video carries a
single count determined by its full length, so the count cannot be varied
independently of the video itself: comparing different counts means comparing
different videos, which also differ in duration, action, and speed. A model’s
error on such a benchmark therefore cannot be attributed to the count rather
than to these correlated factors. The distribution of counts across videos is
also uneven, so some counts are represented by few videos. Diagnosing counting
failures requires varying the count while holding other factors fixed, which
motivates the construction of RepProbe.

setting for studying temporal counting, not because exercise counting is
uniquely difficult. Exercise repetitions are well defined: each repetition is
a complete cycle of a single action, typically beginning and ending in a rest
pose, so repetition boundaries are unambiguous and can be annotated precisely.
RepCount ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides repetition-boundary annotations that allow us to segment videos into clips containing exactly a specified number of complete repetitions. The synthetic set
(Section 3.2 ) complements this choice by testing
whether our findings extend beyond exercise content.

In each source video, a repetition begins when the action leaves a rest pose
and ends when it returns to one, so consecutive rest-pose timestamps define
each repetition as a half-open interval [ start , end ) [\text{start},\text{end}) . We discard
zero-length and non-monotonic intervals and concatenate k ∈ { 1 , … , 20 } k\in\{1,\ldots,20\} consecutive repetitions into a clip (Figure 1 ). Because

complete repetitions and ends at a rest pose. To vary clip position while
holding the action and source fixed, we extract windows from the start,
middle, and end of the source when it contains enough repetitions; redundant
middle windows are omitted for short sources. For a given source and k k ,
these clips contain the same number of repetitions at different positions in
the source; their durations can differ because action speed varies within a
source.

blocks.en:
Real clips confound the periodic signal with object semantics, scene
appearance, and camera variation such as viewpoint and
lighting, so a model or probe could count by exploiting content cues
rather than periodicity itself. To isolate periodicity, RepProbe-Synthetic
contains 10,000 10{,}000 procedurally generated clips in a
controlled setting: the set is balanced across counts ( 500 500 clips for each k = 1 k=1 – 20 20 ), and in every clip a single attribute changes periodically and
completes exactly k k periods, while everything else stays fixed.

Each clip shows simple geometric elements on a plain background (except for
the Textured flash stress condition), and exactly one attribute changes
periodically. The count is therefore defined only by how
many periods the attribute completes: no single frame reveals it, and there is
no object category or action that could evoke a typical count. Every clip lasts 4 4 s regardless of k k (Figure 2 b), so, unlike in real video,
clip duration carries no information about the count.

blocks.en:
The ten families vary what changes periodically (Figure 3 ) and
fall into three groups. Appearance changes alter an element in place: a
disc appears and disappears (Flash), pulses in size (Scale), cycles in hue
(Color change), or morphs through polygons (Shape change). Motion
changes move an element along a path: a bob hops vertically (Bounce), swings
on a pivot (Pendulum), or travels around a ring (Orbit), and a bar sweeps
across a square (Crossing). Stress conditions make the periodic signal
harder to isolate: Textured flash places the same flash on a cluttered,
scene-like background, and Multi object flash distributes the flashes across
several objects that take turns, so that every flash must be counted
regardless of where it occurs. Together, the families test whether a model
tracks periodic change in general or only specific kinds of change, such as
motion.

blocks.en:
Each model is queried with the instruction “ Count the number of
repetitions in this video. Return only an integer. ” A shared, model-agnostic
parser extracts the predicted count k ^ \hat{k} from each response
(App. A.4 ). Responses from which no integer can be extracted
are treated as parse failures and scored as a prediction of 0 0 , so a model
cannot improve its score by failing to answer. For the main comparison across
models, predictions are clipped to [ 0 , 40 ] [0,40] so that rare extreme outputs do not
dominate mean errors. We report mean absolute error (MAE), which is directly
interpretable in repetitions, and normalized MAE ( MAE n \mathrm{MAE}_{n} ), which we
use when comparing across count ranges: MAE = 1 N ​ ∑ i | k ^ i − k i | , MAE n = 1 N ​ ∑ i | k ^ i − k i | k i . \mathrm{MAE}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}|\hat{k}_{i}-k_{i}|,\qquad\mathrm{MAE}_{n}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\frac{|\hat{k}_{i}-k_{i}|}{k_{i}}. We also report exact-match accuracy and off-by-one accuracy (OBO), the
percentage of predictions with | k ^ − k | ≤ 1 |\hat{k}-k|\leq 1 . OBO is standard in
repetition counting ( Dwibedi et al., 2020 ; Hu et al., 2022 ) ; it tolerates
ambiguity at repetition boundaries while still penalizing genuine miscounts.
Results are further broken down by count band: Few ( k = 1 k=1 – 6 6 ), Mid
( k = 7 k=7 – 13 13 ), and Many ( k = 14 k=14 – 20 20 ).

Unless otherwise stated, each model receives 16 16 frames per clip, sampled
uniformly regardless of duration. Cosmos-Reason2 is the exception: it uses its

blocks.en:
We organize our experiments around three questions. (1) How well do
video language models count repetitions, and does performance hold as the
number of repetitions grows? (Section 4.1 ) (2) When
counting fails, is the count absent from the model’s internal state, or
present but not expressed in the generated answer? (Section 4.2 ) (3) Does the decodable count capture the actual repetitions, or does it rely on simpler cues such as video duration or scene content?
(Section 4.3 )

blocks.en:
The behavioral results show that the model produces the wrong count, but not
whether the count is missing from its representation or present but lost on
the way to the answer. To separate these, we read the count in two ways from
the same final-layer state, the one the language head consumes to produce its
answer. The first readout is the model’s answer: the number it generates when
asked. The second is a count probe. We extract the residual-stream activation after
the final transformer block at the last prompt token, the position from which
the language head produces the first answer token, and train a linear
classifier over the 20 20 count classes ( k = 1 , … , 20 k=1,\dots,20 ) on 1,000 1{,}000 labeled
clips. The probe’s prediction is the most probable class. On RepProbe-Real,
training and evaluation clips are split at the source-video level, so the
probe is always evaluated on source videos it has not seen during training;
full details are given in Appendix A.2 .
Because the probe is linear, it
cannot perform nonlinear computation on the state; it can only recover
information that is already linearly present. The language head is itself a
linear map applied to this same state (after normalization), so the probe has
no more capacity than the model’s own readout: any count the probe recovers is
available to the language head in the form it consumes. A gap between the two
readouts therefore locates the failure in the output pathway rather than in
the representation. Both readouts are computed from the same forward pass on
the same frames, so the comparison is not confounded by differences in input.
We study Cosmos-Reason2-8B and Qwen3-VL-8B, the two strongest generalists
(Table 1 ). Because the probe is trained with supervision, we also
test in Section 4.3 whether it reads the count itself or
correlates of it, such as duration, clip position, or scene content.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We introduced RepProbe, a controlled benchmark for studying repetition
counting in video language models, comprising 42K real and synthetic clips
with exact repetition counts and controlled clip properties. Using RepProbe,
we uncovered a systematic high-count collapse in general-purpose video
language models that persists even when temporal coverage is controlled,
while specialist counting models remain accurate. Most importantly, we showed
that in the models we probe, the repetition count is often more accurately
recoverable from the final representation than from the generated answer, and
that this dissociation is not explained by duration, clip position, or scene
content. Together, these findings suggest that repetition-counting failures
arise primarily from the output pathway rather than from an inability to
perceive or encode repetitions. More broadly, our results highlight the
importance of distinguishing representation from readout when evaluating
temporal reasoning in video language models, and suggest that improving output
mechanisms may be as important as improving visual perception for reliable
counting.

blocks.en: A.2 Additional Probe Details
blocks.zh: A.2 其他勘探细节

blocks.en:
For each clip, we run a single forward pass on the prompt and video and record
the residual-stream activation after the final transformer block at the last
prompt token, the position from which the language head produces the first
answer token. The count probe is a multinomial logistic-regression classifier
over the 20 20 count classes ( k = 1 , … , 20 k=1,\dots,20 ), trained on these activations for 1,000 1{,}000 labeled clips; its prediction is the most probable class, and its
class probabilities are those shown in Figure 4 c. On
RepProbe-Real, training and evaluation clips are split at the source-video
level, so that no source video contributes clips to both. Probe activations
and the model’s generated answer come from the same forward pass on the same
input frames. To see how count decodability changes with depth, we also train
probes at earlier layers. All layers are probed with the same training clips,
evaluation clips, and classifier. At the outputs of blocks 0 0 , 18 18 , and 35 35 ,
probe MAE is 2.91 2.91 , 2.51 2.51 , and 2.49 2.49 for Cosmos-Reason2, and 4.09 4.09 , 2.97 2.97 ,
and 3.05 3.05 for Qwen3-VL; the block- 35 35 values match
Table 2 . These results indicate that repetition-count
information becomes substantially more decodable in deeper layers, with most
of the improvement occurring before the final block; however, the near-flat
MAE for Cosmos-Reason2 and the slight degradation at the final layer for
Qwen3-VL suggest that later layers do not necessarily make the count signal
more linearly decodable.

blocks.en: A.3 Detailed Numerical-Output Analysis
blocks.zh: A.3 详细的数字产出分析

blocks.en:
Figure 4 shows the distributions underlying the
numerical-output analysis in Section 4.2 , computed on
RepProbe-Real. Reading the count directly from digit tokens is biased, because
single-digit integers are one token while two-digit integers span several
tokens, and the first token of 10 10 through 19 19 coincides with the digit 1 1 .
We therefore use a length-fair word readout that compares the single-token
number words “one” through “twenty.” This readout can select two-digit
values, yet predictions still concentrate on a preferred number: the mode is
“fifteen” for Qwen3-VL and “eighteen” for Cosmos-Reason2 across the count
range. The concentration is therefore not explained by token-length asymmetry.

blocks.en:
Paired bootstrap confidence intervals are computed by resampling evaluation
clips with replacement and recomputing the paired difference in MAE for each
of 2,000 2{,}000 replicates. Resampling is performed at the clip level because
paired comparisons evaluate the same clips under different readouts.

blocks.en:
Generated responses are parsed with a deterministic numerical parser. If an <answer>...</answer> span is present, we extract the last integer inside
it. Otherwise, we scan upward from the final line and select the first line
consisting solely of an integer after removing trailing punctuation. If neither
rule succeeds, we use the final match of -?\d+ in the
response. No separate chain-of-thought stripping is applied. Responses without
an interpretable count are treated as parse failures and scored as a prediction of 0 0 . On the balanced 10 10 K subset of RepProbe-Real, failure
rates are at most 0.11 % 0.11\% for Cosmos-Reason2, Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, Video-R1,
and VideoChat-R1.5, 0.67 % 0.67\% for LLaVA-OneVision, and 1.50 % 1.50\% for
LongVILA-R1. Responses that were not produced at all are excluded.
